name: Intellectual Property

claims.claim_text: Employment contracts in some companies assign every idea an employee has, whether or not it relates to the job, with the company holding first right to it. The trade is real on both sides: one engineer was paid several times for ideas, but he could not get permission to enter an outside design contest, which is where the arrangement stops being a trade and starts being a restriction.
claims.quote_verbatim: Every thought and idea that they have, they own
claims.episode_title: Analog Components, First Person Flying and Idea Ownership

claims.claim_text: A workable response to a total-assignment clause is to attach an addendum listing every project and idea predating employment, drawn from old notebooks including projects never started, and get the employer to sign it before the contract takes effect. Nobody had done it before at that company and they signed.
claims.quote_verbatim: here's my signed employment contract plus here's the addendum
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Tesla, Checklists and Bullies - Emerging External Eupsychics

claims.claim_text: Even where an assignment clause would never survive a challenge, that only becomes known once a case reaches court, which is why engineers comply with clauses they believe are invalid. The cheap documented workaround beats being right expensively.
claims.quote_verbatim: it takes it until it goes to court in order to, you know, to tell if people are full of crap
claims.episode_title: Tesla, Checklists and Bullies - Emerging External Eupsychics

claims.claim_text: The commonly quoted numbers are roughly $10,000 to obtain a patent and $100,000 to defend it the first time, and only after that defence is it worth anything. A patent is a licence to litigate, and the litigation is the expensive part.
claims.quote_verbatim: $10,000 to get a patent. But $100,000 to defend it for the first time
claims.speaker: Bob Davidson
claims.episode_title: Impedance Matching" with Davidson and Vandenbout - Presbytes Pushing Portfolios

claims.claim_text: A startup has to protect its intellectual property but should not make that its emphasis, and should not expect great IP to keep competitors out. This is advice from someone who had major startup failures and learned the most from them.
claims.quote_verbatim: I wouldn't put my emphasis there or think that I was going to, you know, keep everybody out because of my great IP
claims.speaker: Bob Davidson
claims.episode_title: Impedance Matching" with Davidson and Vandenbout - Presbytes Pushing Portfolios

claims.claim_text: The value of a thing is the idea multiplied by the execution, so a great idea with poor execution is worth very little. Learning to execute is the critical skill, not generating ideas.
claims.quote_verbatim: the value of something is really the idea times the execution
claims.speaker: Bob Davidson
claims.episode_title: Impedance Matching" with Davidson and Vandenbout - Presbytes Pushing Portfolios

claims.claim_text: On products going out to real users, about ninety percent of the execution effort belongs in the last ten percent of the project, because that is where projects fail. Schedules that taper off at the end are mis-planned.
claims.quote_verbatim: 90% of your execution better be in the last 10% of that project because that's when it fails
claims.speaker: Bob Davidson
claims.episode_title: Impedance Matching" with Davidson and Vandenbout - Presbytes Pushing Portfolios

claims.claim_text: Publishing your best work and helping people who ask returns more than it costs, which is the part that practitioners trained on patent-everything-and-keep-it-secret cannot see. The return arrives as problems solved by others and contacts made rather than as licence income.
claims.quote_verbatim: I get back a lot more than I put out there
claims.speaker: Bob Davidson
claims.episode_title: Impedance Matching" with Davidson and Vandenbout - Presbytes Pushing Portfolios

claims.claim_text: The three subsystems of a product differ sharply in how easily they can be copied. Mechanical is the easiest thing in the world to replicate: put it in a laser scanner and identify the materials. Electrical takes more work but is tractable through component identification and reverse engineering.
claims.quote_verbatim: Mechanical is probably the easiest thing in the world to rip off
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Miller - Sudden SinoAmerican Synthesis

claims.claim_text: The recommended software protection for offshore manufacture is an encrypted bootloader programmed at a secure facility with no internet access and workers screened, with the programmed part then consigned to the factory. It lets firmware travel by email instead of physical media and keeps the plaintext out of the factory entirely.
claims.quote_verbatim: have that bootloader encryption programmed at a secure facility where there's no internet
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Miller - Sudden SinoAmerican Synthesis

claims.claim_text: Consigning a security-critical programmed IC also gives supply-chain control: hand the factory a thousand parts and only a thousand products can exist, which closes off a ghost shift running the same product out the back door. The IP protection and the anti-overbuild control are the same mechanism.
claims.quote_verbatim: you know that they can't run a ghost shift having a product come out the back door
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Miller - Sudden SinoAmerican Synthesis

claims.claim_text: Factories change over time and a good one can go bad. A twenty-year veteran of manufacturing in China lost his company when the management at a long-trusted factory changed and the new owner stole his design. Vetting the factory once is not enough; you have to keep meeting the people running it and understand whose business it now is.
claims.quote_verbatim: the new guy that ran it ended up stealing his IP and basically causing him to shut down his company
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Miller - Sudden SinoAmerican Synthesis

claims.claim_text: Excess caution about IP only becomes a problem if it slows you down or stops you doing something; otherwise it pays to be paranoid, because a single client losing its design would be fatal to the firm that let it happen. The test to apply is whether the protection blocks the product getting built.
claims.quote_verbatim: the only reason that being overly concerned about it would be a problem is if it slowed them down
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Miller - Sudden SinoAmerican Synthesis

claims.claim_text: Open source hardware imposes no requirement to publish before you manufacture. Releasing files at the idea stage is a choice; you can equally call a design open and publish the files once the product is manufactured and on sale.
claims.quote_verbatim: You can call it open hardware and then once you're manufacturing and got it on sale, then you can release the design files
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Miller - Sudden SinoAmerican Synthesis

claims.claim_text: Medium-volume hardware typically needs between two and ten million dollars, which usually means venture capital, and venture investors expect protected IP as the condition of that money. That is the structural tension for anyone wanting to build open hardware at that scale.
claims.quote_verbatim: you need anywhere from, you know, two to probably more like 10 million of funding
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Miller - Sudden SinoAmerican Synthesis

claims.claim_text: Anyone can legally take open source hardware files and compete directly against the originator. The protection is a community norm rather than a legal mechanism, and treating the norm as if it were enforceable is the mistake.
claims.quote_verbatim: You're legally allowed to do it
claims.speaker: Ian Danaher
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ian Daniher - Nascent Nonolith Numquid

claims.claim_text: Investors consistently ask an open-hardware company how it is protecting itself and where its IP is. A company that has decided not to play that game has to be prepared for the conversation to end there.
claims.quote_verbatim: everybody wants to know how we're protecting ourselves, where's our IP
claims.speaker: Ian Danaher
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ian Daniher - Nascent Nonolith Numquid

claims.claim_text: Read the terms before sending files to a low-cost board house. At least one low-cost assembly service's terms transfer rights such that the design can be made public, which matters most for work done under a client NDA.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you use your low cost assembly service, you basically sign away rights that they can make this public
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: LEDs and EVs with Mike Harrison

claims.claim_text: The countervailing reality is that a bare board layout is weak protection anyway: strip the components, scan the board, and the design is recovered. The exposure that matters is the firmware and the algorithms, not the copper.
claims.quote_verbatim: I'll just strip all the bits off and scan the board and they've got it anyway
claims.episode_title: LEDs and EVs with Mike Harrison

claims.claim_text: In practice consulting clients rarely demand ownership of the designer's accumulated techniques. Across a long contracting career the closest case was a museum whose policy required enough information to repair or rebuild the hardware itself, which is a documentation requirement rather than an ownership one.
claims.quote_verbatim: None of my customers have ever really been interested in owning any of the IP that I've generated
claims.speaker: Mike Harrison
claims.episode_title: LEDs and EVs with Mike Harrison

claims.claim_text: Work developed under contract usually becomes the customer's property and cannot be resold, but the knowledge transfers: rebuilding the same capability later takes a fraction of the time. The asymmetry is what makes contract work compound rather than reset.
claims.quote_verbatim: most of the stuff you develop is, becomes the intellectual property of your customer
claims.episode_title: High End Audio with Remco Stoutjesdijk

claims.claim_text: A consultant can convert that into a business structure by developing general-purpose hardware and libraries between engagements, then offering the pre-built part under licence while charging normal non-recurring engineering for the customer-specific adaptation. It answers the client who needs something ready immediately, which is a bid a from-scratch consultant simply loses.
claims.quote_verbatim: you pay the NRE on the adaptation, but on the stuff that was pre-developed, you just buy a license
claims.episode_title: High End Audio with Remco Stoutjesdijk

claims.claim_text: The ratio a new consultant faces is roughly ten hours of self-teaching for every billable hour, which is why building a personal library of tested algorithms and platforms is what eventually makes the business stable rather than terrifying.
claims.quote_verbatim: for every hour that you can invoice to a customer, you need to work for 10 hours to actually teach yourself this stuff
claims.episode_title: High End Audio with Remco Stoutjesdijk

claims.claim_text: The working rule practitioners apply to reusing blocks between client projects is that the novel property lives in the whole solution, not in its pieces. It is a rule of thumb rather than a legal opinion, and the boundary genuinely blurs once a firm starts templating.
claims.quote_verbatim: Novel IP is only around the whole solution. The pieces of the solution are just trivial.
claims.episode_title: Moving Down The Stack with Scott Williams

claims.claim_text: A failure-analysis consultancy can make not doing design work into a selling point: it stamps no drawings and retains no rights, which is exactly what lets IP-sensitive startups hand over a problem. Scoping a service to exclude design is an IP strategy as much as a technical one.
claims.quote_verbatim: it gives us a plugin with startups and companies that are concerned about their intellectual property because we don't retain any of that
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Steve Kreuzer

claims.claim_text: Buying an HDL core is priced against engineer-hours, not against the sticker: a real-time, deterministic-latency core quoted at $100,000 to $150,000 was still cheaper than building it internally. Do that arithmetic explicitly before deciding to write it yourself.
claims.quote_verbatim: it was like, you know, $150,000 or $100,000 or something, but that's cheaper than actually developing yourself from scratch
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: NFT Schematics

claims.claim_text: A hazard when buying a core: the vendor may be selling a specification rather than a finished product, and only start writing it once someone buys. Ask what silicon or which customers the core has actually run in before committing a schedule to it.
claims.quote_verbatim: All they had was a speck and, and they went, shit, somebody bought it
claims.episode_title: NFT Schematics

claims.claim_text: The decision rule for buy versus build is differentiation. If your advantage is elsewhere, buying the block is not a problem; write it yourself only where that block is the thing you compete on, and be honest that the from-scratch route is an R&D cost paid now against a payoff years away.
claims.quote_verbatim: buying someone else's IP is not a big deal because you don't need to differentiate based on that IP
claims.episode_title: NFT Schematics

claims.claim_text: Chip vendors build products by assembling prepackaged licensed cores: a processor, a memory controller, peripheral controllers. Understanding a modern part often means understanding which third-party blocks were dropped into it.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's basically a prepacketed version of all these different cores
claims.episode_title: Proemial Passive Poiesis

claims.claim_text: Hard-coding processors and peripherals into FPGA fabric addresses a real limit: internal block RAM is usually only a few kilobytes, so an on-die DDR controller is needed for any design that behaves like a processor. Running out of internal memory is the constraint that pushes designs toward external RAM.
claims.quote_verbatim: when you use block RAM or internal RAM, it's usually limited
claims.episode_title: Proemial Passive Poiesis

claims.claim_text: Licensing a widely available core is a sourcing strategy as much as a technical one: once a design is on a common architecture you can choose among many vendors for the best peripherals or power consumption, and the architecture survives any single supplier disappearing because the IP exists independently of them.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can actually pick the best peripherals you need
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Øyvind Janbu - Feracious Fabless Facilitator

claims.claim_text: A pure IP licensor operates under a structural constraint: it could hire peripheral designers, build its own chips and pay itself no royalty, gaining an immediate price advantage, but that would undercut the licensees who fund it. The business model forbids the obvious move.
claims.quote_verbatim: they could hire a couple of peripheral people and develop IP. And they don't have to pay themselves a royalty
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Tektronix, ChipReport.tv, & the Signal Path - Temperative Tegmen Temperature

claims.claim_text: Chip development starts long before engineering does. Roughly six months went into choosing the architecture, deciding which blocks to build versus license, signing NDAs and negotiating IP contracts before any solid engineering began on one microcontroller.
claims.quote_verbatim: you've got to sign a bunch of NDAs and you've got to get a bunch of contracts for IP
claims.speaker: James Adams
claims.episode_title: Embedded Hardware with the Raspberry Pi Team

claims.claim_text: Integrating flash onto the die is not automatically cheaper. Adding flash to a 40 nm process cost roughly 35 percent more, and the flash then consumes the area where SRAM would have gone, so external flash won on cost and also gave the flexibility to fit any memory size.
claims.quote_verbatim: it was about 35% cost up to add flash to 40 nanometers
claims.speaker: James Adams
claims.episode_title: Embedded Hardware with the Raspberry Pi Team

claims.claim_text: A non-standard process carries a hidden IP cost: because third-party blocks are developed and characterised for the standard variant, using a funky flash process means signing a waiver that the licensed IP may not work. Process choice constrains which blocks you can buy.
claims.quote_verbatim: you also have to sign a bit of a waiver on your IP saying, hey, we're using this slightly funky flash process
claims.episode_title: Embedded Hardware with the Raspberry Pi Team

claims.claim_text: Datasheets often name the licensed block and its exact version, so a peripheral's behaviour and errata are traceable to the vendor IP rather than to the chip company. Reading that line tells you where to look when the peripheral misbehaves.
claims.quote_verbatim: by the time you've done that, we'd probably be onto gen two or something
claims.episode_title: The RP1 and beyond with the Raspberry Pi Hardware team

claims.claim_text: The practical case for a mature architecture over a newer open one is availability and documentation: the licensed cores are easy to obtain, well tested, well documented, and include high-performance options, while the open alternative lacks equivalents and has a long way to go on tool maturity. Competition from the open side has already made the incumbent easier to license from.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's very easy to get hold of ARM IP. It works very well. It's well tested. It's well documented
claims.speaker: James Adams
claims.episode_title: The RP1 and beyond with the Raspberry Pi Hardware team

claims.claim_text: Memory macros on a shared shuttle are licensed foundry blocks that cannot be used in an open project, which is why adding meaningful RAM to a small open tapeout is so hard. The licensing boundary, not the silicon area, is the binding constraint.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's all intellectual property that you can't use for for project like that
claims.episode_title: Lifelong Learning with Bitluni

claims.claim_text: Vendor blocks frequently arrive as an encrypted bitstream with a generated Verilog header rather than as source, so using the block means using the vendor's tool. Whether the output can be extracted and used with open tools is usually undocumented.
claims.quote_verbatim: you get like a very log interface like a header and then the bitstream in one file
claims.episode_title: Lifelong Learning with Bitluni

claims.claim_text: NDA structure blocks reproducibility in chip design research: verifying somebody else's result can require NDAs with three different companies before you can even approach the raw data, which stunts the field's ability to demonstrate that one approach beats another.
claims.quote_verbatim: If you need to sign an NDA with three different companies to even start getting close to
claims.speaker: Tim Ansell
claims.episode_title: Discussing the Open Source PDK with Tim Ansell

claims.claim_text: Bodge wires on an ASIC are close to impossible, so build observability into the silicon: internal ADC sensors and current measurement let a designer find out why a part failed and iterate rather than treating a tapeout as final.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's very hard to, uh, do bodge wires on an ASIC
claims.speaker: Tim Ansell
claims.episode_title: Discussing the Open Source PDK with Tim Ansell

claims.claim_text: Making a chip requires foundry access, IP blocks, EDA software, complementary knowledge and test capability simultaneously. They combine as an AND gate: miss any one and the result is zero, which is the real barrier for small teams rather than any single cost.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you put all that together in a one big end gate, that's what I call it, it's zero in the end
claims.speaker: Mohamed Kassem
claims.episode_title: Fabless Chip Design with Mohamed Kassem

claims.claim_text: Licensing cost belongs in the per-part cost model alongside die area and I/O count. A configuration might come out at $1.62 per part with zero licensing because the blocks are included in the package, while a third-party block enters the same calculation as cents per part, letting several configurations be compared on cost directly.
claims.quote_verbatim: licensing costs $0
claims.speaker: Mohamed Kassem
claims.episode_title: Fabless Chip Design with Mohamed Kassem

claims.claim_text: Foundries have an incentive to accumulate validated customer designs: each retained data converter or block becomes an enablement offered to the next customer, so more available blocks means more business. That is the argument for persuading a foundry to open its process.
claims.quote_verbatim: more IP and more functions means potentially more business
claims.speaker: Mohamed Kassem
claims.episode_title: Fabless Chip Design with Mohamed Kassem

claims.claim_text: What kills FPGA startups is not the first chip but the second. Beyond making designs fit, you must integrate third-party blocks around the chip, build a soft-IP ecosystem, and build a sales channel, with investment rising exponentially as capacity grows, so the first product typically consumes all the money.
claims.quote_verbatim: you probably spend most of the money you can't even build a second chip
claims.speaker: Sammy Cheung
claims.episode_title: Efinix FPGAs with Sammy Cheung

claims.claim_text: A closed-source bootloader can be a deliberate way for a small company to encapsulate the work it put into a product, in a niche shared with much larger competitors. The reasoning is that a bootloader given away removes the reason to buy the board.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's basically a way to encapsulate IP as well
claims.episode_title: Rubber Duck Incarnate

claims.claim_text: An NDA with a silicon vendor can enable a product variant rather than just restrict one: chip security features covered by NDA made a lockable board possible with encrypted firmware and a secure update process, sold alongside a standard version without those features.
claims.quote_verbatim: The chip security features are the main thing covered by the NDA
claims.episode_title: Rubber Duck Incarnate

claims.claim_text: Knockoff phones represent enormous genuine engineering, whatever the trademark on the case: someone laid out the circuit board, ported an operating system and made a GSM stack work. The barrier to producing the hardware had to fall very far before designs came to be treated as freely remixable material.
claims.quote_verbatim: they had to like lay out a circuit board. They had to pour an OS. They had to get this whole thing working. They had to make a GSM stack work
claims.speaker: Bunnie Huang
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Bunnie Huang (2nd)

claims.claim_text: An argument from someone who has shipped open hardware commercially: even without strong patent or copyright protection, an idea can be monetised for long enough to fund the next generation, and the lack of a monopoly forces the designer to stay competitive rather than resting on one product.
claims.quote_verbatim: I'm able to sort of monetize my ideas for a period of time. That's long enough for me to get to the next generation
claims.speaker: Bunnie Huang
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Bunnie Huang (2nd)

claims.claim_text: The cost of long monopoly rights falls on the people who would have moved the field forward and cannot, because they have been shut out of the ecosystem. Perfect protection benefits exactly one narrative.
claims.quote_verbatim: they've been locked out of that ecosystem in a way
claims.speaker: Bunnie Huang
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Bunnie Huang (2nd)

claims.claim_text: A project can be worth building even with no financial return, because the property generated is intuitive fluency with the process rather than any copyright or patent. Eighty units sold at cost bought understanding of the whole flow.
claims.quote_verbatim: I now had, like, intuitive fluency
claims.speaker: Bunnie Huang
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Bunnie Huang (2nd)

claims.claim_text: When users asked who would own designs entered into a hosted tool, the answer that worked was a public page of promises backed by a matching update to the terms of service, so the reassuring page was legally binding rather than marketing. The terms were revised again each time another hosted service had a public incident.
claims.quote_verbatim: I need you to update the terms of, of, of service so that this page is valid
claims.episode_title: Interview with the Upverter Founders - Ramiform Reciprocity Raconteurs

claims.claim_text: What makes hosted design data acceptable is a credible exit: open, documented export formats plus an open source converter to other tools, and servers paid for well in advance. The vendor's framing is that the data has value inside the tool and is dead data outside it, so it is not an asset they would ever try to sell.
claims.quote_verbatim: it comes in an open source file format. It's super documented
claims.episode_title: Interview with the Upverter Founders - Ramiform Reciprocity Raconteurs

claims.claim_text: A deliberate decision not to enforce licences on shared designs: let users declare a licence, but do not track or police forks, because tracking derivation is an impossible complexity problem and becoming an IP enforcement body is not the business.
claims.quote_verbatim: we don't actually enforce it or track it
claims.episode_title: Interview with the Upverter Founders - Ramiform Reciprocity Raconteurs

claims.claim_text: An argument against paid marketplaces for design blocks: giving people a way to monetise work they would not otherwise think valuable is harmful, because most of that work is not special to them and would be better shared. Most of what a designer does to reach a goal is work they would happily have borrowed.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you give people a way to monetize work that they would otherwise not believe has value, you've done a very bad thing for the world
claims.episode_title: Interview with the Upverter Founders - Ramiform Reciprocity Raconteurs

claims.claim_text: Even a small per-block charge kills reuse: as soon as there is a transactional cost on a design block, engineers will not take it, especially when vendors already give away reference designs for free. The friction of a payment exceeds the cost of redrawing the circuit.
claims.quote_verbatim: as soon as you put a dollar transactional cost on that, that's no way
claims.episode_title: Interview with the Upverter Founders - Ramiform Reciprocity Raconteurs

claims.claim_text: Publishing schematic symbols and footprints to a shared cloud library is a real disclosure decision for a corporation, since footprints and symbols reveal which parts are used. A tool whose default policy is that everything created is public forces each company to decide whether that is acceptable rather than assuming it is.
claims.quote_verbatim: everything is public, right? So if you, if you create a symbol or you create a footprint, it's going to be public by default
claims.speaker: Andrew Seddon
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Andrew Seddon - Necessary Networked Novelty

claims.claim_text: Omitting the top silkscreen saves on the order of ten cents a board and one process step. The obscurity it buys is a side effect that some manufacturers cite, but cost is the actual driver.
claims.quote_verbatim: 10 cents per board if you don't get, you know, a top silkscreen on with R1, R2
claims.episode_title: Project Management, Lasers & Robots - Staunch Specialty Sanctanimity

claims.claim_text: The defensible protection boundary in an instrument is the algorithm, not the interface. Pot the algorithm or run it in an encrypted microcontroller, but the output should still be usable data; locking the output as well protects nothing extra and cripples the customer.
claims.quote_verbatim: Put it in an encrypted micro. But the output signal should be, you know, something usable
claims.episode_title: Layouts and Design-Outs

claims.claim_text: A silicon vendor can differentiate on code in ROM rather than on the die: a motor-control family's distinguishing feature was a software encoder that turns current and voltage signals into flux angle, speed and torque, feeding the control algorithms. The premium is charged for the algorithm shipped on the chip.
claims.quote_verbatim: the code in ROM. That's, that's what differentiates them
claims.speaker: Trey German
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Trey German - Launchpad Laden Lodesman

claims.claim_text: Universities generally do not pre-negotiate IP with corporate research sponsors, because nobody knows in advance how valuable the result will be.
claims.quote_verbatim: they don't pre-negotiate any IP
claims.speaker: Jonathan Ellis
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jonathan Ellis

claims.claim_text: One reason companies fund university research is portfolio building: monthly meetings open with whether any new IP was generated, driven by legal departments tracking the pipeline, because the process from filing to grant runs about five years.
claims.quote_verbatim: it takes five years to get all that
claims.speaker: Jonathan Ellis
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jonathan Ellis

claims.claim_text: Universities typically own the IP arising from work they helped fund, and technology transfer can then proceed by selling that IP to a company. Anyone doing sponsored or student work should establish who the owner is before assuming it is themselves.
claims.quote_verbatim: usually a school owns the IP because they help fund it
claims.episode_title: Shonky Stiver Stultiloquence

claims.claim_text: Describing an unprotected idea in a company meeting where people are taking notes creates a real risk that the company patents it. The exposure exists even when the speaker never intended to pursue the idea.
claims.quote_verbatim: what if then that company goes and patents it?
claims.episode_title: Prior Art, Wafer Fabs and Guns - Whimsical Wafer Waffling

claims.claim_text: A genuine market exists for domestic, higher-cost fabrication among customers who cannot let a design leave the building at all, including defence and intelligence work and companies unwilling to send files offshore, alongside customers who simply need very quick turnaround.
claims.quote_verbatim: people who don't want to send their IP outside
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Boat Anchors

claims.claim_text: The extreme version of that requirement is an in-house fab, operated so that the design never leaves the site at any stage of production.
claims.quote_verbatim: they have their own in-house chip fab because they don't want the IP to go out anywhere else
claims.episode_title: Occam's Engineering Razor

claims.claim_text: Manufacturers lock down firmware citing proprietary information, and they sincerely believe the recipe needs that protection, but the same lockdown also limits exposure if someone finds a vulnerability in a machine with real-world consequences. The stated reason and the operative reason can differ.
claims.quote_verbatim: they really do think that they have to protect their secret sauce to that extent
claims.episode_title: Impedance Matching with Michael Ossmann and Dmitry Nedospazov

claims.claim_text: A practitioner ethic on reverse engineering that acknowledges both sides: intellectual property is real and research costs money, but a vendor that sells a device with something hidden inside it has accepted the risk that a buyer will find and exploit it.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you're going to sell us something and you've hidden something inside of there, and if we happen to find a way to exploit it, well, tough tits to you. That was your risk.
claims.episode_title: Robots are coming - Ominous Operational Overhaul

claims.claim_text: A publishing line one hardware writer draws: hardware modifications and teardowns are fair game even when they void a warranty, but license key hacks are not published because those break intellectual property directly. The distinction is between understanding a device you own and circumventing a paywall.
claims.quote_verbatim: I won't publish license key hacks
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Look at nature and meet nerds

claims.claim_text: There are two ways to sell a failing company: on its IP alone, meaning the patents plus any prototypes, systems or code, or on its talent as an acqui-hire, or a combination. Which one applies determines what the founders retain.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's two ways to shop a company
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: The Automation Amish

claims.claim_text: Once a founder takes investment capital, the patents belong to the company and the founder becomes a shareholder like any other. Even patents originally gifted to a founder are signed over as part of the financing, and that structure is deliberate.
claims.quote_verbatim: the company owns the patents
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: The Automation Amish

claims.claim_text: If generated images cannot be copyrighted, a publisher will not invest in the property because it is not defensible and a third party could later force the work down. Whether the output of a tool can be owned determines whether anyone will fund work built on it.
claims.quote_verbatim: They're not going to invest in the IP
claims.episode_title: The Magic of Calipers
